name: Apache Drill
summary: A distributed SQL engine, inspired by Google’s Dremel, that queries JSON, Parquet, CSV files and NoSQL stores in place without defining a schema first.
intro: Drill runs a service called a Drillbit on each node, ideally next to the data, and uses ZooKeeper to keep track of which Drillbits are alive. A client sends SQL from the Drill shell, the web UI, a JDBC driver or the REST API to any Drillbit, which becomes the Foreman for that query: it parses and optimizes the SQL with Apache Calcite, turns the physical plan into major fragments (phases) and splits each into minor fragments, units of work that run as threads on Drillbits close to the data. Drill needs no central catalog. Storage plugins describe each source: file systems (local, HDFS, S3, Azure Blob Storage, SFTP), Hive, HBase, MongoDB, Cassandra, Elasticsearch, Kafka, Druid, Splunk, JDBC databases, HTTP APIs and Google Sheets.

Its main idea is schema on read: Drill discovers the schema while it reads each batch of records, so you can point SQL at a directory of JSON or Parquet files and query nested fields straight away, with no `CREATE TABLE`. Directory names become the columns `dir0`, `dir1` and so on, which it uses to skip partitions. One query can join a file in S3 with a Hive table and a MongoDB collection. The project is still maintained by a small group of committers: 1.22.0, released in June 2025, dropped Java 8, and work since then has added materialized views, an Accumulo plugin and Java 25 support, though no newer release had shipped by October 2026.
strengths: Queries self-describing data such as JSON and Parquet in place, with no schema definitions or loading step
One SQL query can join across files, Hive, HBase, MongoDB, Kafka and JDBC databases through storage plugins
A hierarchical columnar data model handles nested and changing data, with functions such as `FLATTEN` for nested arrays
An embedded JDBC driver, a web UI and a REST API, so tools can use it like a database (the ODBC driver comes from a vendor, not the project)
limits: Activity is low: few regular contributors, and the last release (1.22.0) is from June 2025
Schema discovery at read time can fail or slow down on inconsistent files, such as a JSON field that changes type
Its Hadoop-era design, with long-running Drillbits and ZooKeeper, is more work to run than serverless engines like Athena or embedded ones like DuckDB

story: In 2010 Google described Dremel, which ran ad-hoc aggregations over trillion-row tables of read-only nested data in seconds. Hadoop’s MapReduce gave high throughput but not the low latency people wanted for exploring data. In 2012 engineers at MapR Technologies, with contributors from Concurrent and Drawn to Scale, proposed Drill to the Apache Software Foundation as an open-source take on Dremel: interactive analysis of large, nested datasets. It entered the Apache Incubator in September 2012 and became a top-level project in November 2014.

Drill 1.0, the first production-ready release, came out in May 2015. That year Tomer Shiran, one of Drill’s first committers, and Jacques Nadeau, who ran MapR’s distributed systems team, founded Dremio. Drill itself kept going as a community project; in recent years a small group of committers, with Charles Givre the most active, has fixed bugs and added storage plugins, format readers and, in 2026, materialized views.

choices.why: Self-describing formats like JSON and Parquet already carry their structure, so requiring table definitions first would slow down exploration and break on data that changes shape.
Each storage plugin supplies its own metadata, so Drill can query many Hive metastores, HBase tables and file systems at once without copying their catalogs.

choices.choice: A peer-to-peer cluster of identical Drillbits
choices.why: Any Drillbit can take a query and act as its Foreman, so there is no master node, and Drillbits can sit on the data nodes for locality.

timeline.text: Drill enters the Apache Incubator in September, proposed by MapR engineers
Graduates to a top-level Apache project in November
Drill 1.0, the first production-ready release, in May
Drill 1.22.0 drops Java 8 and the MapR plugin (June)
Materialized views and Java 25 support land on the main branch
